title: How an AI Music Style Finder Works: Features, Classifiers and a Toy Python Example
author: Tania Alwan
summary: By Tania Alwan Upload a track, get back "lo-fi hip hop, 0.82" or "synthwave, 0.64". An AI music style finder looks like magic from the outside, but inside it is a fairly classic machine learning pipeline: turn audio into numbers, train a classifier on labelled examples, and output probabilities. This post walks through how that pipeline works, which datasets researchers use, where these systems break, and then builds a tiny style classifier with librosa so you can see the moving parts. Spoiler: the toy gets a perfect score on its own data, and then falls apart the moment the audio changes. That is the most useful lesson in the whole post. What an AI music style finder is trying to do In research, this task is usually called music genre recognition (MGR) or genre classification, part of the wider field of music information retrieval (MIR). A style finder typically does one of two things: Single-label classification: pick one genre from a fixed list (rock, jazz, hip hop...) Multi-label tagging: score many tags at once, such as genre, mood, instrumentation or era, because real songs rarely fit one box Either way, the output is a set of scores. A threshold or a "top 3" list turns those scores into what the user sees. The datasets behind most genre research Two public datasets come up again and again: GTZAN. Introduced by Tzanetakis and Cook in their 2002 paper "Musical genre classification of audio signals", it contains 1,000 half-minute excerpts labelled in ten categories. Bob Sturm's analysis, "The GTZAN dataset: Its contents, its faults, their effects on evaluation, and its future use" , describes it as the most-used public dataset for evaluating music genre recognition, and catalogues its faults: repetitions, mislabelings and distortions. FMA (Free Music Archive). Defferrard et al. released a much larger dataset of 106,574 tracks from 16,341 artists, arranged in a hierarchical taxonomy of 161 genres, with full-length audio, metadata and pre-computed features, plus baselines for genre recognition. The lesson from Sturm's work is worth remembering whenever you see a high accuracy number: a benchmark score is only as meaningful as the data behind it. Features: what the model listens to Classic style finders start from hand-crafted audio features computed over short frames (tens of milliseconds), then summarised over the clip: MFCCs (mel-frequency cepstral coefficients): a compact description of the spectral envelope, roughly "timbre" Spectral centroid: where the "centre of mass" of the spectrum sits; bright, distorted or cymbal-heavy music tends to score higher Zero-crossing rate: how often the waveform crosses zero, a rough proxy for noisiness Onset strength and tempo: how percussive the track is and how fast the beat is Chroma: energy per pitch class, useful for harmony and key Summary statistics such as the mean and standard deviation over time turn a variable-length track into a fixed-length vector a classifier can use. The librosa library computes all of these in a few lines. Classifiers: from random forests to deep networks Broadly, there are two families: Feature + classifier. Extract features like the ones above, then train an SVM, k-nearest neighbours, a random forest or a small neural network. Fast, interpretable and easy to debug. Learned representations. Feed a (mel) spectrogram, or even the raw waveform, into a convolutional or transformer model and let it learn its own features. These end-to-end approaches need a lot of labelled audio, and the FMA authors cite the limited availability of large audio datasets as a hurdle for this kind of feature and end-to-end learning, which is one reason they built FMA. Commercial "AI music style finder" tools rarely publish their models, training data or evaluation, so treat their confidence scores as rough hints rather than verdicts. The limitations you should know about Genre is fuzzy. Labels are cultural, overlapping and change over time. Two experts can disagree about whether a track is "indie pop" or "bedroom pop", so a model trained on their labels inherits that disagreement. Datasets have faults. Repeated tracks, mislabelled excerpts and artist overlap between training and test sets can inflate accuracy. Sturm's GTZAN analysis is the classic example. Shortcuts. A model can learn cues that correlate with a label in the training data (recording quality, loudness, a particular studio sound) rather than anything musical. Channel effects. Compression, phone speakers, live recordings and EQ change exactly the features the model relies on. The toy below shows how dramatic that can be. A toy AI music style finder in Python The script generates its own synthetic "styles" so it runs without downloading any dataset: ambient (slow pad, no drums), dance (kick on every beat at 120 to 130 BPM plus a bright synth) and rock (slower kick plus a clipped, noisy "guitar"). It extracts MFCCs, spectral centroid, zero-crossing rate, onset strength and tempo with librosa, then trains a random forest. This is a toy. It recognises the differences I built into the clips. It says nothing about real songs. pip install librosa scikit-learn import numpy as np import librosa from sklearn . ensemble import RandomForestClassifier from sklearn . model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn . metrics import confusion_matrix SR = 22050 rng = np . random . default_rng ( 42 ) STYLES = [ "ambient" , "dance" , "rock" ] def toy_clip ( style , dur = 4.0 ) : """Synthetic 'style' clips (NOT real music): each style differs in tempo, percussion and timbre, the cues real classifiers also use.""" t = np . arange ( int ( SR * dur ) ) / SR root = rng . uniform ( 110 , 220 ) if style == "ambient" : # slow, soft pad, no drums y = sum ( np . sin ( 2 * np . pi * root * r * t ) for r in ( 1 , 1.5 , 2 ) ) y *= 0.5 + 0.5 * np . sin ( 2 * np . pi * 0.25 * t ) else : bpm = rng . uniform ( 120 , 130 ) if style == "dance" else rng . uniform ( 90 , 110 ) beat = 60 / bpm y = np . zeros_like ( t ) for start in np . arange ( 0 , dur , beat ) : # kick drum on every beat n = int ( start * SR ) ; m = min ( len ( t ) - n , int ( 0.15 * SR ) ) y [ n : n + m ] += np . sin ( 2 * np . pi * 60 * t [ : m ] ) * np . exp ( - t [ : m ] * 30 ) if style == "dance" : # bright saw-like synth y += 0.3 * sum ( np . sin ( 2 * np . pi * root * k * t ) / k for k in range ( 1 , 15 ) ) else : # "distorted guitar": clipped harmonics + noise y += 0.4 * np . clip ( 3 * np . sin ( 2 * np . pi * root * t ) , - 1 , 1 ) y += 0.05 * rng . standard_normal ( t . size ) y += 0.01 * rng . standard_normal ( t . size ) return ( y / np . max ( np . abs ( y ) ) ) . astype ( np . float32 ) def features ( y ) : mfcc = librosa . feature . mfcc ( y = y , sr = SR , n_mfcc = 13 ) centroid = librosa . feature . spectral_centroid ( y = y , sr = SR ) zcr = librosa . feature . zero_crossing_rate ( y ) onset_env = librosa . onset . onset_strength ( y = y , sr = SR ) tempo = librosa . feature . tempo ( onset_envelope = onset_env , sr = SR ) [ 0 ] return np . r_ [ mfcc . mean ( 1 ) , mfcc . std ( 1 ) , centroid . mean ( ) / 1000 , zcr . mean ( ) , onset_env . mean ( ) , tempo / 100 ] labels = np . repeat ( np . arange ( 3 ) , 60 ) X = np . array ( [ features ( toy_clip ( STYLES [ l ] ) ) for l in labels ] ) X_tr , X_te , y_tr , y_te = train_test_split ( X , labels , test_size = 0.3 , random_state = 0 , stratify = labels ) clf = RandomForestClassifier ( n_estimators = 200 , random_state = 0 ) . fit ( X_tr , y_tr ) print ( f "test accuracy: {clf.score(X_te, y_te):.2f}" ) print ( "confusion matrix (rows = true):" ) print ( confusion_matrix ( y_te , clf . predict ( X_te ) ) ) # Same clips, but heard through a "phone speaker": low-pass at 3 kHz def phone ( y ) : S = np . fft . rfft ( y ) ; f = np . fft . rfftfreq ( y . size , 1 / SR ) S [ f > 3000 ] = 0 return np . fft . irfft ( S , n = y . size ) . astype ( np . float32 ) X_phone = np . array ( [ features ( phone ( toy_clip ( STYLES [ l ] ) ) ) for l in labels ] ) print ( f "accuracy on low-passed clips: {clf.score(X_phone, labels):.2f}" ) print ( "predicted styles on low-passed clips:" , dict ( zip ( STYLES , np . bincount ( clf . predict ( X_phone ) , minlength = 3 ) . tolist ( ) ) ) ) I ran it with Python 3.13, librosa 1.0.1, NumPy 2.5.4 and scikit-learn 1.9.1. My run printed: test accuracy: 1.00 confusion matrix (rows = true): [[18 0 0] [ 0 18 0] [ 0 0 18]] accuracy on low-passed clips: 0.33 predicted styles on low-passed clips: {'ambient': 0, 'dance': 180, 'rock': 0} Your numbers may differ slightly with other library versions. The first two results look perfect, because the three toy styles are easy to separate. The last two lines are the interesting part: the same clips, simply low-passed at 3 kHz as if played through a small speaker, drop to 0.33 accuracy, which is chance level for three classes, and every single clip is labelled "dance". Nothing about the rhythm or the harmony changed; only the timbre did. That is the channel-effect problem from the section above, in miniature. Things worth trying: Print clf.feature_importances_ to see which features the forest leans on Add low-passed clips to the training set (data augmentation) and test again on a different filter Replace the synthetic clips with a real dataset such as the small FMA subset, and you will quickly see why real genre recognition is much harder Takeaways An AI music style finder is a classifier (or tagger) that maps audio features to genre or style scores Features range from MFCCs, spectral centroid and tempo to learned spectrogram representations; models range from random forests to deep networks Benchmarks such as GTZAN have known faults, and models can be fooled by recording conditions, so treat any single style score as a hint If you are analysing tracks rather than labelling them, style is usually only one of the things you want to know. Tools such as the Voicestars BPM and key finder or librosa itself can estimate tempo and key, which are often more useful than a genre label when you are building a playlist, a DJ set or a cover version. title: Ubuntu removed a root CA. Node 22.23.2 still trusts it: comparing CA lists by public key
author: Jose Pollman
summary:
On 30 October, apt on my Ubuntu 24.04 container installed ca-certificates 20260816ubuntu0.24.04.1 . Its changelog has one line that matters here: * Blacklist the following CA cert due to intermediate cert compromise (LP: #2171507) + "emSign ECC Root CA - G3" That is the root above the intermediates with tiny private keys that I wrote about in October . The system store dropped it. The question I wanted answered was narrower: what on this machine still trusts it? Answering it takes two steps. Ask each runtime which list it reads, then compare the lists by public key. Step 1: ask each runtime where it looks Python's ssl module reads whatever OpenSSL was built to read: import ssl print ( ssl . get_default_verify_paths ( ) ) ctx = ssl . create_default_context ( ) print ( ctx . cert_store_stats ( ) ) print ( any ( "emSign ECC Root CA - G3" in str ( c [ "subject" ] ) for c in ctx . get_ca_certs ( ) ) ) DefaultVerifyPaths(cafile='/usr/lib/ssl/cert.pem', capath='/usr/lib/ssl/certs', openssl_cafile_env='SSL_CERT_FILE', openssl_cafile='/usr/lib/ssl/cert.pem', openssl_capath_env='SSL_CERT_DIR', openssl_capath='/usr/lib/ssl/certs') {'x509': 120, 'crl': 0, 'x509_ca': 120} False /usr/lib/ssl/cert.pem is a symlink to /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt , so plain ssl follows the distro: 120 roots, no G3. That stops being true the moment you pip install requests . The Requests docs say it "uses certificates from the package certifi", and certifi ships its own cacert.pem , frozen at whatever certifi version you have. Node is the interesting one. Since 22.15 it has tls.getCACertificates(type) , which returns the list for each source: bundled (the copy compiled into the binary), system , extra (from NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS ), and default , the list TLS clients actually use. This script prints all four and checks for G3: const tls = require ( 'tls' ) ; const { X509Certificate } = require ( 'crypto' ) ; const spki = ( p ) => new X509Certificate ( p ) . publicKey . export ( { type : 'spki' , format : 'der' } ) . toString ( 'base64' ) ; const distinct = ( pems ) => new Set ( pems . map ( spki ) ) . size ; const hasRoot = ( pems , cn ) => pems . some ( ( p ) => new X509Certificate ( p ) . subject . split ( '
' ) . includes ( `CN=${cn}` ) ) ; console . log ( `node ${process.version}, NODE_USE_SYSTEM_CA=${process.env.NODE_USE_SYSTEM_CA ?? 'unset'}, flags: ${process.execArgv.join(' ') || 'none'}` ) ; for ( const t of [ 'default' , 'bundled' , 'system' , 'extra' ] ) { const pems = tls . getCACertificates ( t ) ; console . log ( ` ${t.padEnd(8)} ${String(pems.length).padStart(4)} entries, ${String(distinct(pems)).padStart(3)} distinct keys, G3: ${hasRoot(pems, 'emSign ECC Root CA - G3')}` ) ; } On Node 22.23.2, run three ways (the bundled , system and extra lines are the same in all three runs, so I cut them from the second and third): node v22.23.2, NODE_USE_SYSTEM_CA=unset, flags: none default 145 entries, 145 distinct keys, G3: true bundled 145 entries, 145 distinct keys, G3: true system 360 entries, 120 distinct keys, G3: false extra 0 entries, 0 distinct keys, G3: false node v22.23.2, NODE_USE_SYSTEM_CA=1, flags: none default 505 entries, 149 distinct keys, G3: true ... node v22.23.2, NODE_USE_SYSTEM_CA=unset, flags: --use-openssl-ca default 0 entries, 0 distinct keys, G3: false ... Three things in that output matter. The default list is the bundled one. The Node docs describe it as "a snapshot of Mozilla CA store that is fixed at release time". 22.23.2 came out on 28 July (per Node's release index ), so its snapshot has G3, and no OS update can change that. NODE_USE_SYSTEM_CA=1 adds, it does not subtract. The docs for --use-system-ca say Node uses the system store "along with" the bundled one, and they are blunt about the consequence: "Node.js currently does not support distrust/revocation of certificates from another source based on system settings." So 145 bundled plus 360 system entries gives 505, which collapses to 149 distinct keys: the 145 bundled roots plus four roots that only the system store has. G3 is still in. Turning on the system store only helps with roots the bundle is missing, never with roots the distro removed. --use-openssl-ca reports an empty default list, and it still works. In that mode the default list leaves out the bundled roots, as the docs say it will, and the OpenSSL store that Node verifies against does not show up in it. So I checked that it really verifies against the system store rather than against nothing: node --use-openssl-ca -e "require('https').get('https://www.rfc-editor.org/', r => console.log(r.statusCode, r.socket.authorized))" SSL_CERT_FILE = /dev/null SSL_CERT_DIR = /nonexistent node --use-openssl-ca -e "require('https').get('https://www.rfc-editor.org/', r => console.log(r.statusCode)).on('error', e => console.log(e.code))" 200 true UNABLE_TO_GET_ISSUER_CERT_LOCALLY The 360 system entries for 120 roots are not a bug either. The docs warn that the array "may contain duplicates if the same certificate is repeatedly stored in multiple sources", and Node reads both the bundle file and the certificate directory. Count distinct keys, not entries. Step 2: compare the lists by public key Comparing files by hash tells you nothing, and comparing by name is fragile. A CA can reissue a root with the same key under a new certificate, so the key is the identity that matters. The script below hashes each certificate's SubjectPublicKeyInfo and walks just enough DER to find the subject and the key, with the standard library only: """Compare CA bundles by public key. Usage: python3 trust_inventory.py REF.pem OTHER.pem ...""" import hashlib , re , sys from base64 import b64decode PEM = re . compile ( rb "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----(.+?)-----END CERTIFICATE-----" , re . S ) def tlv ( buf , i ) : """Return (tag, start of value, end of value) for the DER element at i.""" tag , n = buf [ i ] , buf [ i + 1 ] i += 2 if n & 0x80 : size , n = n & 0x7F , int . from_bytes ( buf [ i : i + ( n & 0x7F ) ] , "big" ) i += size return tag , i , i + n def fields ( buf , start , end ) : """Split a SEQUENCE body into its elements as (tag, start, end) of the whole element.""" out = [ ] while start < end : tag , vs , ve = tlv ( buf , start ) out . append ( ( tag , start , ve ) ) start = ve return out def parse ( der ) : """Return (SPKI SHA-256, subject CN or O) for one DER certificate.""" _ , s , e = tlv ( der , 0 ) # Certificate _ , s , e = tlv ( der , s ) # tbsCertificate f = fields ( der , s , e ) if f [ 0 ] [ 0 ] == 0xA0 : # skip the explicit [0] version f = f [ 1 : ] subject , spki = f [ 4 ] , f [ 5 ] # serial, sigAlg, issuer, validity, subject, spki name = { } for oid , label in ( ( b "\x55\x04\x03" , "CN" ) , ( b "\x55\x04\x0a" , "O" ) ) : k = der . find ( b "\x06\x03" + oid , subject [ 1 ] , subject [ 2 ] ) if k != - 1 : _ , vs , ve = tlv ( der , k + 5 ) name [ label ] = der [ vs : ve ] . decode ( "utf-8" , "replace" ) return hashlib . sha256 ( der [ spki [ 1 ] : spki [ 2 ] ] ) . hexdigest ( ) , name . get ( "CN" ) or name . get ( "O" ) def show ( sign , names , limit = 6 ) : for n in names [ : limit ] : print ( f " {sign} {n}" ) if len ( names ) > limit : print ( f " ... and {len(names) - limit} more" ) def load ( path ) : data = open ( path , "rb" ) . read ( ) certs = [ b64decode ( b "" . join ( m . split ( ) ) ) for m in PEM . findall ( data ) ] return len ( certs ) , dict ( parse ( c ) for c in certs ) ref_path , * others = sys . argv [ 1 : ] ref_count , ref = load ( ref_path ) print ( f "{ref_path}: {ref_count} certificates, {len(ref)} distinct keys (reference)" ) for path in others : count , roots = load ( path ) extra = sorted ( roots [ k ] for k in roots . keys ( ) - ref . keys ( ) ) missing = sorted ( ref [ k ] for k in ref . keys ( ) - roots . keys ( ) ) print ( f "
{path}: {count} certificates, {len(roots)} distinct keys" ) print ( f " trusted here but not in the reference: {len(extra)}" ) show ( "+" , extra ) print ( f " in the reference but not here: {len(missing)}" ) show ( "-" , missing ) To get Node's bundle into a file, node -e "process.stdout.write(require('tls').rootCertificates.join('
'))" > node-bundled.pem . Then compare it, today's certifi release ( 2026.11.20 ) and an older certifi copy I found inside a desktop app, all against the system store: /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt: 120 certificates, 120 distinct keys (reference) node-v22.23.2-bundled.pem: 145 certificates, 145 distinct keys trusted here but not in the reference: 29 + AffirmTrust Commercial + AffirmTrust Networking + AffirmTrust Premium + AffirmTrust Premium ECC + Atos TrustedRoot 2011 + COMODO Certification Authority ... and 23 more in the reference but not here: 4 - SECOM TLS ECC Root CA 2024 - SECOM TLS RSA Root CA 2024 - Telia EC TLS Root CA v3 - Telia RSA TLS Root CA v3 certifi-2026.11.20.pem: 113 certificates, 113 distinct keys trusted here but not in the reference: 0 in the reference but not here: 7 - Buypass Class 2 Root CA - Buypass Class 3 Root CA - Certigna Root CA - QuoVadis Root CA 1 G3 - QuoVadis Root CA 3 G3 - emSign ECC Root CA - C3 ... and 1 more vendored-certifi-in-app.pem: 121 certificates, 121 distinct keys trusted here but not in the reference: 1 + emSign ECC Root CA - G3 in the reference but not here: 0 The same Ubuntu changelog accounts for all 29 extra roots in Node's bundle. The June package ( 20260601~24.04.1 ) lists 24 roots removed in its update to Mozilla bundle 2.86, DigiCert Global Root CA and the four AffirmTrust roots among them. The October package removes four more with bundle 2.90 and blacklists G3. Node 22.23.2 was released on 28 July and still carries every one of them. certifi goes the other way: the current release trusts fewer roots than Ubuntu and lacks seven that Ubuntu still ships, two other emSign roots among them. The old copy inside the app is byte-identical to certifi 2026.07.22, and it still has G3. The fix for Node is an upgrade Node did remove G3. The commit "crypto: update root certificates to NSS 3.131.1" (20 October) lists emSign ECC Root CA - G3, emSign Root CA - C1 and emSign ECC Root CA - C3 as removed. I fetched src/node_root_certs.h at the current release tags: v22.23.5 116 roots G3: no v24.22.3 118 roots G3: no v26.13.1 118 roots G3: no Run through the same comparison, the 22.23.5 bundle has only two roots the Ubuntu store lacks (Atos TrustedRoot 2011 and the Chunghwa Telecom ePKI root) instead of 29. So on 22.x the answer is 22.23.5 or later. The other Node on this machine, 20.20.2, bundles 144 roots including G3 and has no getCACertificates at all. It will not get a fix: Node 20 reached end of life on 30 April 2026 ( release schedule ), and 20.20.2 from 24 March was its last release. If you would rather your Node processes follow the distro's decisions, --use-openssl-ca does that. NODE_USE_SYSTEM_CA=1 does not. The copies you did not install on purpose The last step is a plain find : find ~ /opt /usr \ ( -name cacert.pem -o -name tls-ca-bundle.pem -o -name ca-bundle.pem \ ) -type f 2 > /dev/null It turned up 296 files on this machine. 284 were named cacert.pem , and 264 of those sat in uv's package cache. Of the 20 outside the cache, 15 still list G3: certifi inside three virtualenvs and a uv tool, pip's own vendored certifi in three uv-managed Python installs and one virtualenv, six copies in container image layers, and the desktop app from above. The other five: botocore's own cacert.pem , a game that ships one, and three Flatpak bundles. I did not work out which of these each program reads at runtime, so treat the count as places to check, not as 15 open holes. What I would check on any machine node -p "process.version + ' ' + require('tls').rootCertificates.length" on every Node you run, then compare with a current release of the same line. The OS store does not reach the bundled list. python -m certifi in every virtualenv that uses Requests, and the certifi version pinned in your lock files. Container images: each one carries the ca-certificates package and any certifi from the day it was built. The find above, then the SPKI comparison on anything it turns up. The distro did its job on 30 October. The other copies change only when you upgrade the thing that ships them, and nothing warns you that a copy is out of date. Written with AI assistance from my own notes and test results. I checked every fact and command before publishing.

title: Designing Resilient Third-Party API Integrations for Production
author: tanmay kuamr chaurasia
summary: Most third-party API integrations do not fail because of flawed syntax or poor business logic. They fail because the system was engineered under the assumption that the external service would always behave predictably. When writing integration code, handling authentication and sending basic requests is only about 20% of the effort. The remaining 80% involves accounting for real-world failures: transient network glitches, unexpected rate limits, silent response schema updates, and sudden vendor downtime. If you only code for the happy path, a minor vendor disruption will quickly cascade into your application. Here is how to build resilient API integrations that survive unpredictable failure modes. Step 1: Enforce Strict Timeouts and Retry Strategies Never make an HTTP request without an explicit timeout. A hanging connection to an external vendor can exhaust your application's worker pool, bringing down your entire backend service. Combine strict connection timeouts with an exponential backoff strategy for transient errors (such as 502, 503, or rate-limiting 429 status codes). Exponential backoff ensures you do not overwhelm an already struggling API with rapid retry loops. Here is a production-ready implementation in Python using httpx and tenacity : import httpx from tenacity import retry , stop_after_attempt , wait_random_exponential , retry_if_exception_type class ExternalAPIError ( Exception ) : """Custom exception for non-retryable API failures.""" pass @retry ( stop = stop_after_attempt ( 4 ) , wait = wait_random_exponential ( min = 1 , max = 10 ) , retry = retry_if_exception_type ( ( httpx . TimeoutException , httpx . HTTPStatusError ) ) , reraise = True ) def fetch_vendor_data ( endpoint_url : str , api_key : str ) -> dict : headers = { "Authorization" : f "Bearer {api_key}" } # Define explicit connect and read timeouts timeout = httpx . Timeout ( timeout = 5.0 , connect = 2.0 ) with httpx . Client ( timeout = timeout ) as client : response = client . get ( endpoint_url , headers = headers ) # Raise HTTPStatusError for server errors or rate limits to trigger retries if response . status_code in ( 429 , 502 , 503 , 504 ) : response . raise_for_status ( ) if response . status_code != 200 : raise ExternalAPIError ( f "API request failed with status: {response.status_code}" ) return response . json ( ) Step 2: Validate Response Schemas explicitly External vendors frequently push unannounced updates, rename attributes, or omit fields from JSON payloads. If your application expects user.email and suddenly receives user.contact_email , untyped code will crash deep inside your business logic. Validate incoming responses at the network boundary using a strict data validation layer. If the vendor alters their response structure, fail early at the point of ingestion. from pydantic import BaseModel , EmailStr , ValidationError class VendorUserPayload ( BaseModel ) : user_id : str email : EmailStr account_status : str def parse_vendor_response ( raw_json : dict ) -> VendorUserPayload : try : return VendorUserPayload ( ** raw_json ) except ValidationError as error : # Schema drift detected; alert monitoring tools immediately raise ExternalAPIError ( f "Response payload schema validation failed: {error}" ) Step 3: Implement Circuit Breakers for Vendor Downtime If an external vendor experiences an extended outage, continually making requests wastes compute resources and increases latency for your users. A circuit breaker pattern monitors outbound request failure rates. When failures cross a specific threshold, the circuit "trips" open, immediately failing subsequent requests or returning cached/fallback data without attempting the network call. Once the cooldown period passes, the breaker allows test requests through to check if the vendor has recovered. Step 4: Log Structured Context for Observability Debugging integration failures without context is inefficient. Generic logs like Error 500 provide no actionable information during an incident. Always log structured, contextual metadata for outbound integration requests: Correlation IDs to trace the request through your microservices Endpoint paths and HTTP methods Status codes and rate-limit response headers (e.g., x-ratelimit-remaining ) Redacted error bodies for inspection Ensure sensitive data, secret tokens, and personally identifiable information (PII) are scrubbed before writing to log stores. Assume Failure by Design Reliable software systems are not built by hoping third-party services stay online. They are built by assuming external dependencies will fail, and placing strict, defensive boundaries around them. title: Uptime Kuma 2 with uptime-kuma-api 1.x: socket timeouts and a dead healer
author: Christian Anderson
summary: I've got a small Python script I call the healer. Every 5 minutes it logs in to Uptime Kuma, asks which monitors are down, and tries to fix them. If a monitor is down for 2 runs in a row it restarts the service. If that doesn't bring it back, it reboots the container, with a cap on how many reboots it'll do in an hour. It's the bit of my homelab that's meant to fix things while I'm asleep. On 9 August 2026 I opened its log. It was about 2.4 MB of Python tracebacks. It had been dead for months. Not dead once, either. Dead twice, for two completely different reasons, one after the other. And next to it, a second watcher of mine had the opposite problem: it was far too keen, and it was restarting a perfectly healthy service every 10 minutes. Same lesson in both, which is why they're in one post. Phase 1: the wrong password, ~1,915 times The first block of failures was boring. authIncorrectCreds , about 1,915 of them. The healer had the wrong Kuma password. The fix was to give it the right one. It reads the password from the environment, then from a local .env file, and deliberately never from my secrets manager at runtime. That's on purpose. The box it runs on had flaky outbound connections back then, and a monitoring script shouldn't need a network round-trip to check whether the network is up. Fixed that, ran it, and it still failed. Just differently. Phase 2: Kuma says yes, the client never hears it The second block was about 1,892 socketio TimeoutError failures. This is the one that had really been killing it for months. The odd thing was where it failed. The socket connected instantly. The login went through. Kuma's own server log said so: [AUTH] Successfully logged in user ... But the acknowledgement of that login never reached the Python client. It sat waiting for an answer the server thought it had already sent, then timed out. The cause is a version mismatch. The server was Uptime Kuma 2.4.0 . The library was uptime-kuma-api 1.2.1 , which is written for Kuma 1.x. It mostly works against Kuma 2, which is what makes it sneaky. It just doesn't reliably get that login ack. Things that didn't help, so you don't have to try them: A longer timeout. 300 seconds failed exactly like 15 seconds. The ack isn't slow, it's not coming. Downgrading python-socketio. I tried going from 5.16.3 down to 5.11.4 and 5.9.0. Nothing changed reliably. What does help is a fresh connection. The ack lands on most attempts, just not all of them. So the fix is retries, each one with a brand new client and a short timeout: for attempt in range ( 1 , KUMA_CONNECT_TRIES + 1 ) : api = None try : api = UptimeKumaApi ( KUMA_URL , timeout = KUMA_TIMEOUT_SEC ) api . login ( KUMA_USER , KUMA_PASSWORD ) return api except Exception as e : last = e if api is not None : try : api . disconnect ( ) except Exception : pass if attempt < KUMA_CONNECT_TRIES : time . sleep ( KUMA_RETRY_WAIT_SEC ) raise RuntimeError ( . . . ) 5 tries, 15 seconds each. If every attempt fails it alerts Discord at most once an hour and exits 1, instead of dumping a traceback every 5 minutes. After the change it logged in 8 runs out of 8 , usually on attempt 1 to 3. If you're debugging this yourself, the step that settles it is reading the server's log, not the client's. The client just says timeout. The server tells you the login worked, and that's what points you at the protocol instead of the password or the network. The bug hiding behind it With the healer actually running again I watched it for a bit, and one monitor (my 3D printer) went down, then "all up", then down again across three runs. It wasn't flapping. The healer was lying. Fetching a monitor's recent heartbeats can time out the same way the login does. The code wrapped that call in except: pass . So a failed fetch meant no "down" beat was found, which meant the monitor counted as up . That reset its consecutive-down count to zero, so it might never reach the threshold of 2 that triggers a fix at all. Now that call retries 3 times, and if it still fails the monitor is reported as unknown , not up. Unknown monitors keep their down-count. And after a restart, if the re-check comes back unknown, it never escalates to rebooting a container. Not being able to ask isn't the same as it being fine, and it isn't the same as it being broken either. Meanwhile, the opposite problem Same day, a different script. I've got a security watcher I call Sentinel that runs every 10 minutes and checks my CrowdSec engine is alive, over SSH. For 24 hours it had been posting this to Discord about every 10 minutes: 🚨 CrowdSec LAPI was **<empty>** and restarting CrowdSec each time. CrowdSec was never down. Its journal showed nothing but clean stops, always right on the cron boundary. That was my own script restarting it. The empty string was the clue. The check did systemctl is-active crowdsec over SSH and restarted anything that wasn't active . But systemctl is-active prints the state even when the unit is dead. It exits non-zero and still prints failed or inactive . Empty output only ever means one thing: I didn't get an answer at all. The SSH connection had failed, and the script was reading "couldn't reach the box" as "the service is dead". The fix is a function that returns None when the box can't be reached, and a real state otherwise: def unit_state ( host , unit ) : rc , out , _ = ssh_retry ( "root" , host , f "systemctl is-active {unit}" ) out = ( out or "" ) . strip ( ) . splitlines ( ) [ - 1 ] . strip ( ) if ( out or "" ) . strip ( ) else "" return out or None SSH gets 3 tries with a 3 second wait. A real non-active state still restarts. None posts an alert saying no restart was attempted because the health is unknown, and leaves the service alone. The same bug was in two other checks. The one that counts failed logins on my SSO box recorded 0 when it couldn't read the log. Then the next run saw the real count, worked out a massive jump, and shouted brute-force attack. Now it skips the run and keeps the old number. The failed-SSH check got the same treatment. After deploying it: zero restarts, normal "all clear" runs, and a real triple SSH failure produced the "unknown" alert instead of a restart. Why was SSH failing in the first place? Probes from that box were failing to every other box about 20 to 30% of the time. That turned out to be a whole other story, two containers sharing one network identity, which I covered in my DHCP lease churn post . But the watcher should never have depended on SSH being perfect. One more thing I found Even if the healer had been alerting all along, I wouldn't have heard. The helper that posts to Discord was fetching an old bot token and getting 401 Unauthorized on every send. Quietly. So the healer's alerts about its own failures were failing too. It reads the working token now, and I checked a send comes back true. I also added log rotation for both scripts, because 2.4 MB of tracebacks is how this hid for so long. Small gotcha there: on my boxes /var/log is root:syslog with 775, and logrotate skips files under it as "insecure permissions" unless you add su root syslog to the config. What I'd do differently Three answers, not two. Up, down and unknown. Any check that can't tell "down" from "couldn't ask" will eventually either restart something healthy or ignore something broken. Mine managed both at once. Empty output is a fact. If a command always prints something when it works, empty means it didn't run. Treat it as its own case. Check the client library supports your server's major version. The library I was using targets Kuma 1.x. Against Kuma 2 it works just well enough to fool you. Monitor the monitor. A healer that's been dead for months looks exactly like a homelab where nothing broke. How long would it take you to notice your own auto-fix had stopped? For me it was months. 🤖 Drafted with AI assistance from my own homelab notes, logs and repos, and fact-checked against them before publishing.

title: Put a Dash app behind Google sign-in
author: nwon19
summary: Dash is Plotly's Python framework for interactive data dashboards, and AI coding tools write it well. This is how to make sure only people in your company can open what they write. Where the app comes from The steps are the same whichever tool wrote the app. Tool Where the app is Before you start Claude on the web or desktop In the conversation Ask Claude for the full project as files, including requirements.txt . A Dash app needs a Python server, so it cannot run as an Artifact. Claude Code In a folder on your machine Ask it to add the sign-in below and to read secrets from environment variables, never from the code. Codex or Cursor In your repository or a cloud task The same. Their own app sharing signs visitors in with their own accounts, so this guide applies when viewers should use your Google sign-in. The rule that matters Signing someone in with Google proves they have a Google account. It does not prove they work for you. Every option below needs a second check that limits sign-in to your organization, and that check is where most mistakes happen. Google's OpenID Connect documentation is direct about two traps: The hd request parameter only shortcuts the sign-in screen for one domain. Google says not to rely on it to control access, "as client-side requests can be modified". The domain of the email claim does not identify members of a Google Workspace organization. Check the hd claim inside the ID token instead. Google says that claim "can be trusted", because it is part of a token Google signed. Option 1: sign-in inside the app, with dash-auth dash-auth is Plotly's authentication package for Dash. Version 2.3.0 (March 2024, per PyPI ) includes OIDCAuth , which works with any OpenID Connect provider, Google included. Plotly describes the package as feature-complete: it takes bug fixes but no new features. In Google Cloud In a Google Cloud project that belongs to your organization, set the app's audience to Internal . Google's audience page says this limits sign-in "to members of the organization". People outside it get an org_internal error. Create an OAuth client of type Web application. Add the redirect URI: your app's address followed by /oidc/callback (for local testing, http://localhost:8050/oidc/callback ). Google requires an exact match. Keep the client ID and secret out of the code. Put them in environment variables. Step 1 is the access rule, and it is the simplest one to get right. If the project cannot be Internal, the app has to check the hd claim of every ID token itself. dash-auth's README does not show how to read claims, so confirm how your version exposes them before you rely on that check. In the app pip install dash-auth import os from dash import Dash , html from dash_auth import OIDCAuth app = Dash ( __name__ ) app . layout = html . Div ( "Revenue by region" ) auth = OIDCAuth ( app , secret_key = os . environ [ "SESSION_SECRET" ] ) auth . register_provider ( "google" , token_endpoint_auth_method = "client_secret_post" , client_id = os . environ [ "GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID" ] , client_secret = os . environ [ "GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET" ] , server_metadata_url = "https://accounts.google.com/.well-known/openid-configuration" , ) if __name__ == "__main__" : app . run ( debug = False ) Anyone who opens the app is sent to Google first. SESSION_SECRET signs the session cookie: a long random string, the same on every server, kept out of the repository. Things to know Public pages are opt-in. dash-auth has public_routes and add_public_routes for pages anyone may see. Leave them out unless you mean it. Groups need your own wiring. dash-auth has group helpers ( check_groups , protected_callback ), but its README shows them only with fixed lists of users. Google's ID token claims list has no groups claim, so restricting to a Google group means calling Google's Admin SDK yourself. Each app is its own client. Ten apps means ten OAuth clients, ten secrets and ten redirect URIs to keep track of. Option 2: sign-in in front of the app, with oauth2-proxy oauth2-proxy runs beside the app, sends people to Google, and passes only signed-in requests through. The app has no login code. --email-domain limits sign-in to addresses on your domain. --google-group limits it to members of one or more Google groups. Per the Google provider page , this needs a service account with domain-wide delegation, the Admin SDK API turned on, and an admin account to impersonate. Membership is checked at sign-in and again each time the token refreshes, about once an hour. The group check is worth the setup. It means removing someone from the group closes the app to them within the hour, without anyone editing the app. Option 3: Identity-Aware Proxy, if the app runs on Google Cloud If the app runs on Cloud Run, App Engine or behind a Google Cloud load balancer, Identity-Aware Proxy can sit in front of it. Access is granted per person or group with the "IAP-secured Web App User" role. Google's own caveat: check that the app cannot also be reached directly, around the proxy. What none of the options solves Sign-in answers who can open the app. A security team will ask more: Where is the database password? Usually in an environment variable the builder set, and knows. Keeping database credentials out of apps covers the alternatives. Who owns this app, and what happens to it when they leave? What did it ship with? Nobody scanned the code for leaked keys or vulnerable packages. How many are there? Each app is set up by hand, and nothing lists them. First published on intrium.dev . intrium is governed hosting for the apps your team builds themselves. The steps above work with or without it.

title: Review and Rating Trends: Read Past the Star Average
author: ExtensionBooster
summary: Originally published on Extenify . Review and rating trends tell you far more about a browser extension or mobile app than the single star number on its store listing. Two products can both show 4.4 stars while one is thriving and the other is slowly losing its users. Here is a practical way to read the signals around that average, so you can tell which problems to fix first. Weigh the average by its rating count Before you react to the average, check how many ratings sit behind it. The count decides how much any change in the average actually means. Small listings: a few ratings can move the average by a whole star. Skip the average and read each review on its own. Large listings: with thousands of ratings, the average hardly moves even after a rough week. So when it does move, a lot of users have changed their minds, and you should look into it. The count is a signal in its own right. Steady growth means people are engaging with the listing. A sudden spike means something pushed many users to rate at once. A falling count is unusual, but stores do sometimes remove ratings, so note it when it happens rather than leaving it unexplained. Read the distribution The average squashes the whole distribution into one number. Look at the shape of the star bars instead: Shape of the bars Likely story Mostly 5s, small tail of 1s A healthy product with a small group hitting one specific bug Big 5s and big 1s, little in between Polarised: great for some users, broken for others Clustered on 3s and 4s Useful but forgettable, and users see room to improve 1s growing while 5s stay flat A new problem hitting part of your audience The polarised shape deserves the most attention. It usually points to something that differs between users: their browser version, a site your extension integrates with, their device or their region. Fixing that one failure can lift the average more than shipping a new feature. Compare stores against each other If you publish to Chrome, Edge, Firefox, the App Store or Google Play, comparing stores side by side often tells you more than any single timeline. When the same code scores clearly lower on one store, the cause is probably specific to that store: Build lag. A slower review queue left an older version live there. Platform behaviour. An API acts differently in one browser, such as Firefox compared with Chrome. Audience. Users on that store expect something different from your product. Stale listing. The description or screenshots promise something the current version no longer does. Problems that only show up on one store are often the quickest wins, because the comparison already tells you where to look. Read reviews for patterns Any single review is noisy. Some users leave one star over a feature they misunderstood, and others give five stars before they have really used the product. The value is in what repeats across many reviews. Tag complaints by theme. Use a short fixed list: a broken feature, performance, a missing feature, pricing, permissions or privacy, and confusion about how something works. After 20 or 30 reviews, one or two themes usually stand out. Check the timing. A theme that appears in several reviews within a few days almost always has a cause you can find, such as a release, a change on a website the extension depends on, or a browser update. A theme that has been there for months is a product decision you have been putting off. Mine the praise too. Positive reviews show which features users care enough to mention. Use their wording in your listing copy, and protect those features in your next redesign. Track the history and automate alerts A store listing only shows today's numbers. To see a trend, you need a daily record. Once you have it, three questions cover most situations: Is the average moving, and is the rating count large enough for that move to matter? Is it happening on every store, or only on one? Did it start near a release, a listing edit or an outside event? Checking all of this by hand stops working as you grow. These are the events worth being alerted to on the day they happen: New reviews, so you read low-star reviews while they are fresh An unusual burst of reviews, which usually means something has happened The rating dropping or recovering, so you catch a slide early and can confirm a fix worked For routing these signals to the right people without flooding your channels, see this guide to setting up change alerts for app and extension listings . Key takeaways Read the rating count before you trust the average. The shape of the distribution shows a lot, and a polarised shape usually means one fixable failure. If one store scores lower than the others, look for a cause specific to that store. Group reviews by theme and timing, and read what users praise as well as what they complain about. Keep a daily history and set alerts for drops, recoveries and bursts of reviews. The full article on reading review and rating trends across app and extension stores has charts and more examples, and Extenify's multi-store analytics for extensions and apps collects this history for you. What signal in your reviews or ratings has warned you about a problem before your own monitoring did?

title: Samsung Securities: Hackers Got Into a Website Feedback Form and Took 8,241 Customers' ID Files. Where Do the Files Your Customers Upload End Up?
author: HackerMe
summary: Originally published at security.hackerme.ai . Samsung Securities said hackers got into a website feedback form and took files from 8,241 customers. Where do the files your customers upload end up? On 23 November 2026, the brokerage told reporters what it had found. Unauthorized access had reached the "Voice of Customer" intake system on its website, on the afternoon of 21 November. Seoul Economic Daily and SBS, citing the company, said attackers took the files customers had attached to their inquiries. Yonhap also reported the same number of clients. What was in those files According to Seoul Economic Daily and SBS, the files covered up to 13 data fields. Those fields included names, account numbers, addresses, contact details and driver's license numbers. The fields involved vary by customer. The company said it will tell each affected customer which of their fields the attackers took. Seoul Economic Daily also said customers can check through a "Personal (Credit) Information Leak Inquiry" menu on the company's website. What the company did, as reported Samsung Securities blocked the IP address and suspended the Voice of Customer intake service, Seoul Economic Daily reported. SBS said the company also put firewall blocks in place. Both papers, and Yonhap's shorter account, said the firm notified regulators. Those bodies included the Financial Supervisory Service and the Korea Internet & Security Agency. Chief Executive Park Jong-moon issued an apology, according to Seoul Economic Daily. The company said it has found evidence of the incident only in the Voice of Customer system so far. It also said the incident does not affect customers who have never submitted a request there. It is investigating the cause and reviewing its other systems. If the company confirms actual damage, it said it will compensate in line with the law and its internal standards. Yonhap placed the incident in a wave of cyberattacks against South Korean financial firms in recent months. SBS noted a recent surge of hacking incidents in the financial sector. None of the three reports named an attacker. They also did not describe how the attackers got in, or say anyone later sold those files. So I am not going to fill those gaps. Why this matters if you run a small site Still, you do not need to be a brokerage. Almost every small-business site has a contact form, a support form, or a quote form. Many of those forms accept a file. Customers attach a copy of an ID, an invoice, a contract, or a screenshot of a problem. Those files often sit somewhere on the site, in an inbox, or in a folder the form created. If anyone can open that folder with a direct link, the file is no longer just a message to you. The same is true if too many people can open the form's admin page. I am not saying this is how the Samsung Securities incident happened. The reports do not say. I am saying this is the part a shop owner can check this week, without waiting for a full investigation. I keep thinking about the quote form on a small shop's site, because I have seen owners treat it as a mailbox. It is also a filing cabinet for other people's documents. What to check this week I would start with these checks. 1. Where the uploads are stored, and whether a direct URL or a public folder exposes them Ask your developer or host where the contact, support and quote forms save those files. Then, without circulating a customer's real file, check whether a direct link to an upload opens in a private window. Also check whether anyone can list or search the folder. If they can, treat that as urgent. I wrote earlier about a Contact Form 7 file upload flaw and about file upload security on a website . Those are different bugs and different checklists. The habit is the same: know where the file goes after someone hits send. 2. How long you keep the files, and delete the old ones Decide how long you actually need a customer's ID copy or invoice. If you have finished the job, delete the attachment. A form that keeps every file "just in case" turns into a pile of other people's documents. 3. Who can open the form's admin side List everyone who can read those submissions. That list may include staff, a freelancer, an old agency login, or a plugin support account. Remove people who no longer need access. A stronger sign-in check on those accounts is worth it. None of these checks proves you are safe. They also will not tell you whether someone already copied a file. They only shrink the pile and the number of people who can see it. Customers will still blame your name if someone takes their file, even when a vendor or a form tool sits in the middle. I wrote about that after a store app that could see customer addresses and after a payment vendor that held card data . It also helps to know what your host handles for website security, and what you still need to check . FAQ Did the reports say how the attackers got into the website feedback form? No. They describe unauthorized access, or an external intrusion, to the Voice of Customer intake system on the website. They do not describe the method. Do not treat a guess as a fact. If I never use a "Voice of Customer" form, am I in the clear? The company said the incident does not affect customers who have never submitted a request in that system. That limit applies to this incident, not to your site. If your contact, support or quote form accepts files, you still have a place where customer documents can sit. Does passing these checks mean my site is safe? No. Checking the place you store uploads, deleting old files, and limiting who can open the form admin reduces what is lying around. It does not prove that nobody can reach those files. It also does not prove that nobody ever copied a file. Will a free website scan find the files customers upload? Not reliably. A scan can be one outside check of what a stranger sees on your site. It will not reliably show the place you store uploads, how long you keep them, or who can open the form admin. It does not prove you are safe. A simple first step The work that matters is the three checks above. A scan is only a side look at your public site. You can run a free website security scan to see what a stranger sees on your own website. It will not inspect your upload folder or your form admin, and it does not prove you are safe. But if you want a website vulnerability scanner that takes a few minutes and no setup, it is a reasonable way to check your website's security before you call your developer.

title: How I Built a Pre-Merge SSR SEO Audit Gate for Next.js 16 Content Pages
author: Felix M
summary: When you ship programmatic or template-driven content pages in Next.js, next build and ESLint will happily pass while your pages quietly fail in Google Search Console as "Crawled - currently not indexed." I ran into this firsthand while building and scaling structured reference pages for Tarot Fortune Cards on Next.js 16 (App Router) + React 19 + next-intl . The UI looked great in Chrome, Lighthouse was green, and every route compiled cleanly—yet inspecting the raw HTML that crawlers actually receive exposed four subtle bugs that were silently hurting indexation. Instead of doing manual spot-checks after deployment, I turned those failure modes into an automated two-stage pre-merge SEO gate (static repo check + live Vercel preview SSR HTML check). Here is what it catches and the exact patterns you can drop into your own Next.js workflow. Why Checking in Chrome DevTools Lies Modern Next.js apps mix Server Components, Client Components, dynamic imports, and next/image . When you inspect a page in Chrome DevTools, you are looking at the post-hydration DOM . Search crawlers do render JavaScript eventually, but initial crawl discovery, canonical evaluation, and structured data extraction still heavily favor clean first-response SSR HTML . If your primary content, comparison tables, or FAQ answers only appear after client hydration—or if your template accidentally repeats 30% of the same sentences across sibling routes—indexation slows down dramatically. The 4 Silent Bugs Our Pre-Merge Gate Catches 1. Cross-Page Boilerplate Overlap (Template Cannibalization) Even when every page is hand-written or carefully edited, shared intros, transition paragraphs, disclaimers, and CTA blocks add up fast. Across a cluster of sibling reference pages, it is surprisingly easy to end up with 25–40% identical sentences , which looks like thin templated content to search engines. Our static audit extracts visible prose from every page in a batch and enforces a hard < 15% pairwise normalized sentence overlap ceiling before a branch is allowed to merge: import re from itertools import combinations def normalize_sentences ( text : str ) -> set [ str ] : # Split on sentence boundaries and ignore very short UI labels (< 6 words) raw = re . split ( r "(?<=[.!?])\s+" , text ) sentences = set ( ) for s in raw : cleaned = re . sub ( r "[^a-z0-9\s]" , "" , s . lower ( ) ) . strip ( ) if len ( cleaned . split ( ) ) >= 6 : sentences . add ( cleaned ) return sentences def pairwise_overlap ( pages : dict [ str , str ] , threshold : float = 0.15 ) -> list [ tuple ] : failures = [ ] sets = { slug : normalize_sentences ( txt ) for slug , txt in pages . items ( ) } for a , b in combinations ( sets . keys ( ) , 2 ) : union = sets [ a ] | sets [ b ] if not union : continue jaccard = len ( sets [ a ] & sets [ b ] ) / len ( union ) if jaccard >= threshold : failures . append ( ( a , b , round ( jaccard * 100 , 1 ) ) ) return failures Running this before merge caught duplicate framing sentences in our first draft batch immediately—forcing us to rewrite shared section leads into page-specific explanations and cutting overlap down to under 5%. 2. Above-the-Fold Media Accidentally Lazy-Loaded or Oversized Template pages often share a single hero or visual component. One careless loading="lazy" attribute (or leaving an unoptimized 300 KB+ PNG in /public ) will silently push mobile LCP past 3 seconds across every route using that template. Our pre-merge rule for primary visual assets: Convert every primary visual to WebP and enforce a hard <= 60 KB file-size cap in the static repo check. Require explicit width and height attributes on the rendered tag to eliminate CLS. Assert on the raw SSR HTML that the above-the-fold visual does not contain loading="lazy" . 3. Broken Heading Hierarchy & Missing Server-Rendered Structured Data In Next.js App Router, we keep route files thin and pull typed metadata and structured content from a central config module: import { setRequestLocale } from 'next-intl/server' ; import { TarotSeoLandingPage } from '@/shared/blocks/tarot/seo-landing-page' ; import { createTarotSeoMetadata , getTarotSeoPage , } from '@/shared/lib/tarot-seo-pages' ; export const generateMetadata = createTarotSeoMetadata ( 'king-of-swords-yes-or-no' ) ; export default async function KingOfSwordsYesOrNoPage ( { params , } : { params : Promise < { locale : string } > ; } ) { const { locale } = await params ; setRequestLocale ( locale ) ; return ( < TarotSeoLandingPage page = { getTarotSeoPage ( 'king-of-swords-yes-or-no' ) } /> ) ; } Then, against the deployed Vercel Preview URL (before merging to main ), the second stage of our script fetches the raw HTML directly—no headless browser—and validates: HTTP 200 + canonical matches the exact production slug URL. Title length ( 30–60 chars) and meta description ( 120–160 chars), with sitewide uniqueness so two routes never accidentally share the same . Exactly one <h1> , and zero skipped heading levels ( h1 -> h2 -> h3 , never jumping straight from h1 to h4 ). Core content in raw HTML : minimum word count threshold, semantic HTML <table> for quick-scan facts, and FAQ questions rendered inside real heading tags ( <h3> ) rather than collapsed client-only accordions that vanish when JS is disabled. Valid JSON-LD : parses every <script type="application/ld+json"> block and verifies both BreadcrumbList and FAQPage parse cleanly as valid JSON with non-empty items. sitemap.xml & robots.txt check : confirms the new slug is actually included in sitemap.xml and not accidentally blocked by noindex or Disallow . If you want to see what the passing raw SSR output looks like in practice, run view-source: on our King of Swords Yes or No guide —every heading, quick-reference table, FAQ answer, < 60 KB eager WebP asset, and JSON-LD block is present in the initial server response before React hydrates. 4. Accidental Regression on Existing Top-Ranking Pages This is the one most developers forget until traffic drops. When you refactor a shared layout or metadata helper to support new content pages, it is dangerously easy to alter the <title> , meta description, or <h1> of your existing top-performing URLs . Our static audit keeps a short list of protected slugs (our top organic landing pages) and diffs their resolved title , description , and h1 against origin/main before every PR merge. If a refactor touches any protected page's TDH unexpectedly, the check fails immediately with FAIL > 0 and blocks the merge. The Two-Stage Checklist Summary Stage Target What It Blocks 1. Static Repo Gate Git branch before push Duplicate titles/descriptions, pairwise sentence overlap >= 15% , local WebP > 60 KB , missing inbound links, mutations to protected top-ranking pages 2. Live Preview SSR Gate Raw HTML from Vercel Preview Non-200 status, wrong canonical, noindex leaks, multiple <h1> s, loading="lazy" on hero images, invalid JSON-LD, missing sitemap.xml entry Running both stages takes under 5 seconds locally and eliminates an entire class of "why didn't Google index my new Next.js pages?" debugging two weeks later. What pre-merge checks do you run on your Next.js or programmatic SEO templates before pushing to production?

title: Converting Multi-Line Identifiers Across SQL, TypeScript, CSS & Env Vars Without Wrecking Acronyms or Line Endings
author: Muhammad Ahmad
summary: Every full-stack feature touches at least five different naming conventions before it ships. You define columns in Postgres, map them into TypeScript interfaces, expose a REST endpoint or URL slug, wire up CSS custom properties, and configure feature flags in .env . Here is the exact same concept across 8 developer naming formats: Format Example Where You Use It snake_case max_retry_count PostgreSQL columns, Python (PEP 8), Rust, Ruby camelCase maxRetryCount JavaScript/TypeScript variables, JSON API keys, Java methods PascalCase MaxRetryCount React components, TypeScript types/interfaces, C# public members kebab-case max-retry-count URL slugs, CSS classes/variables, HTML attributes, CLI flags CONSTANT_CASE MAX_RETRY_COUNT .env variables, global constants dot.case max.retry.count Spring Boot properties, i18n keys, YAML/JSON config paths path/case max/retry/count File routes, S3 object keys, component directories COBOL-CASE MAX-RETRY-COUNT HTTP headers, legacy mainframe/COBOL identifiers The 3 Annoyances When Batch-Converting Lists Converting one variable name by hand takes two seconds. Converting 40 database columns into TypeScript fields or .env keys is where mistakes creep in: Collapsed newlines: Many quick online converters treat a 40-line list as one giant paragraph, turning all 40 columns into a single 300-character string. Broken acronyms: Pasting httpResponseTime or userIPv6Address into a basic regex turns it into h_t_t_p_response_time or user_i_pv6_address . If you're in VS Code, extensions like Change Case handle multi-cursor edits right inside your editor. When you're copying lists out of a browser, Notion doc, or spreadsheet and want a zero-install local utility with Preserve Lines on by default, acronym-aware splitting across all 8 developer formats, and 1-click Trim Lines / Remove Blank Lines / CRLF → LF cleanup without any network uploads, KivaroTools' in-browser text case converter runs entirely in client-side JavaScript memory (no cookies, no localStorage , no API calls). It's part of the KivaroTools browser utility suite . Quick Sanity Checklist Normalize whitespace ( Trim Lines + CRLF → LF ) before converting multi-line lists. Double-check digit boundaries (like v2 vs. v_2 ) when generating environment variable names or URL slugs.
