title: How we carry a prompt gallery into a React image editor
author: Albert
summary: A gallery thumbnail is a surprisingly ambiguous starting point for an image editor. Someone looking at a studio photo of a coffee cup might want the lighting recipe for a different product. Someone else might want to remove a spoon from that exact photograph. Those clicks should open different editor states. We ran into this while building the prompt gallery for PomiGen . Here is the small routing decision behind our three entry points. Gallery action Initial text Initial reference image Make something similar The example prompt None Edit this image Empty, ready for an instruction The selected image Use as reference The example prompt The selected image Pass an identifier through the URL The gallery link carries a prompt ID. The other two actions add a mode and an image index. The index matters when an example has several images: if a reader is looking at the third one, using the cover image would silently change their input. The workbench fetches the example by ID. If an image index is missing or out of range, it falls back to the first image. An edit starts with a blank instruction because the caption that generated the original cup is rarely the instruction someone needs to remove the spoon. Initialize the form once Applying a fetched prompt to editable React state has a trap. If the query refreshes after someone has started typing, an effect can overwrite their changes. Our workbench records which prompt ID has already initialized the text field. A refresh of that same record leaves the draft alone. Image selection is handled separately because it also depends on the selected image index. Three checks worth trying in your own editor: Open the second image in a gallery entry and choose Edit . Check that the second image arrives with an empty instruction. Open Make something similar , change a sentence, and trigger a query refresh. Check that your edit survives. Open Use as reference . Check both the input image and the text before generating anything. You can test all three transitions without spending a generation credit. Inspecting the inputs catches a routing mistake that a plausible-looking generated image can easily hide. Written with AI assistance using our project's implementation.

title: From User Interface to Agent Interface. How Ready Is Your Own Product for Agents?
author: Tetiana Anisimova
summary: The user interface we're used to is becoming a thing of the past. More and more of the work happens behind it, and people step in only when a decision is needed. Here's what that means if you build developer tools, run infrastructure, or ship SaaS in 2026. Watch a developer work with a coding agent for an afternoon and count the dashboards they open. Often the answer is close to zero until something breaks. The agent reads the repo, runs the tests, queries the logs, and asks for permission when it's about to do something expensive. The human reviews a diff, approves a plan, and answers a question or two. For decades we designed software for eyes and hands. Now a growing share of our "users" are models that never see a button. They see tool names, JSON schemas and error messages. That is the agent interface , and in 2026 it matters as much as the UI. The examples below come from DevOps and cloud infrastructure, where the stakes (and the bills) are real. At the end, you'll find a practical checklist to see how ready your own product is for agents. In short An agent interface is the set of tools, schemas, permissions and messages that lets an AI agent use your product without a screen. MCP (Model Context Protocol) has become the standard way to expose that interface. Traditional UI shrinks to approvals, exceptions and trust. What is an agent interface? An agent interface is how software presents itself to an AI agent instead of a person. A UI offers screens, menus and forms. An agent interface offers verbs (tools), the shape of their inputs (schemas), rules about who may call them (permissions), and the feedback the agent gets back (results and errors). The Model Context Protocol is the plug that made this practical. A product ships one MCP server, and Claude Code, Cursor, ChatGPT or VS Code can all talk to it. Anthropic counted more than 10,000 active public MCP servers by December 2025. By the July 2026 spec release , the official Tier 1 SDKs were approaching half a billion downloads a month. The same release moved MCP to a stateless core, so a server can run behind an ordinary load balancer. That's the moment a protocol becomes infrastructure. Why the traditional UI is fading (and why it isn't dying) The clearest signal is usage. In the same release post, Honeycomb reported that nearly 20% of its monthly interactive queries now come from agents. So almost one in five "people" asking an observability tool a question doesn't have eyes. Analysts agree. Gartner estimates that up to $234 billion of enterprise application spending is exposed to "agentic arbitrage" by 2030, as agents finish tasks across systems and skip the interfaces in between. A polished interface, Gartner argues, no longer sets a product apart. So is UI dead? No, and the proof comes from the protocol itself. In January 2026, MCP shipped its first official extension, MCP Apps , which lets a tool return an interactive view (a chart, a form, an approval step) right inside the chat. The ecosystem built for agents immediately needed a way to show humans something. That's where UI is going. It stops being the place where work happens and becomes the place where people decide. Everything else moves behind tools. Five shifts when you design for agents instead of people User interface Agent interface Unit of design Screen Tool (a verb) Navigation Menus and tabs Permissions and scopes Validation Inline form hints Schema plus actionable errors Confirmation "Are you sure?" dialog Destructive hint plus human approval Onboarding Product tour Tool descriptions History Activity page Audit log 1. Clicks become tool calls A five-step wizard is a UI artifact. To an agent, it's one tool call with five parameters. If a capability lives only behind a button, agents can't use it. Neither can the customers who work through agents. Good tools are narrow and named after outcomes. Here's the kind of definition we'd want for a staging operation. { "name" : "scale_deployment" , "description" : "Scale a deployment in dev or staging. Never touches production. Ask the user before scaling to zero." , "inputSchema" : { "type" : "object" , "properties" : { "namespace" : { "type" : "string" , "enum" : [ "dev" , "staging" ] } , "deployment" : { "type" : "string" } , "replicas" : { "type" : "integer" , "minimum" : 0 , "maximum" : 5 } } , "required" : [ "namespace" , "deployment" , "replicas" ] } , "annotations" : { "destructiveHint" : true , "idempotentHint" : true } } Look at what does the work. The enum keeps the agent out of production. The maximum caps the cost. The description tells the model when to stop and ask. None of it needs a single pixel. 2. Error messages become the UI A person who sees 403 Forbidden opens the docs. An agent retries, guesses, or gives up. For an agent, the error message is the only UX it gets, so write it like a hint from a senior colleague. Compare two responses to the same mistake. // Bad { "error" : "invalid replicas" } // Good { "error" : "replicas=12 is above the staging limit of 5. Ask the user to pick a value from 0 to 5." } 3. Confirmation moves out of the modal "Are you sure?" dialogs train people to click Yes. An agent calling a tool never sees the dialog, so confirmation has to live in the contract. MCP tool annotations let a server mark a tool as read-only or destructive, and a well-behaved client knows when to pause and ask. DevOps already has great approval surfaces, and none of them is a modal. A terraform plan output is one. A pull request diff is another. The agent does the typing, and the human reviews a precise description of what will change. The diff is the new form. 4. Every action needs an end People close tabs and go home. Agents don't. An agent that starts a GPU instance for a test run has no instinct to stop it at 6 p.m. So anything an agent can start should carry an end time or a budget from the moment it's created. Not a nightly script that sweeps up later. A lease that ends by design. We compared schedules, alarms and leases in How to stop EC2 instances automatically when nobody is using them , and the same logic applies to dev and staging databases . 5. Permissions become navigation In a UI, what you can't do hides in a grayed-out menu. In an agent interface, the role is checked on every call. Treat the agent as a new kind of user with its own narrow rules, not as a copy of you with all your keys. That's also why we argue for running coding agents on a separate, hardened machine instead of your laptop. A real example with Claude Code and a cloud VM Here's how this looks in our own product. Idlefy keeps dev and staging VMs off by default. You lease a machine for a set time, it starts, and when the lease ends, it stops itself. Leases are exposed through a remote MCP server, and connecting it to Claude Code takes one command (sign-in is OAuth in the browser, no API key). claude mcp add --transport http idlefy https://mcp.idlefy.com/mcp/ After that, the "UI" is a sentence. "I need the c6i.2xlarge in us-east-1 for two hours to run the integration suite." The agent calls list_vms to find the machine, then lease_vm for the 120 minutes you asked for. The end time is fixed when the lease starts. If the run needs longer, the agent extends the lease when you tell it to. What the agent can't do matters just as much. Idlefy's tools give it no AWS credentials and no shell on the machine, and the agent doesn't stop or delete anything on its own initiative. Tools are marked read-only, additive or destructive, and your role is re-checked on every request. And the visible UI? It shrank to a warning. Twenty and five minutes before the lease ends, the person (not the agent) gets a heads-up to save work or extend. The agent handles the routine steps, the rules are built into the tools, and you only step in when there's a real decision to make, like whether to keep the machine running a bit longer. The full setup is in Start an EC2 instance from Claude Code (and stop it automatically) . A checklist for agent-ready products Save this for your next planning session. Every important UI action has an API or MCP tool. If it's button-only, agents can't reach it. Tools are named after outcomes , like lease_vm or scale_deployment , not after endpoints. Schemas carry the guardrails. Enums, minimums and maximums beat paragraphs of docs. Errors tell the agent what to do next , including when to ask the human. Destructive tools are marked and gated. Read-only and destructive should never look the same. Anything an agent starts has an end. A lease, a TTL or a budget. Auth is scoped to the agent. OAuth with narrow tokens, no shared static keys. Humans see decisions, not dashboards. Approvals, diffs and timely warnings beat another chart. Every agent action is logged. Who asked, what ran, and until when. The interface is becoming a contract The user interface isn't going away. It's splitting in two. The work moves into tools, schemas and permissions that agents call through MCP. People will see fewer screens, but the ones they do see will matter more, because that's where they make the decisions that shouldn't be left to an agent. So the question for your 2027 roadmap isn't "Do we need an AI chatbot?" It's "Could an agent use our product safely without ever seeing it?"

title: Four Agent Architectures from Leading AI Companies
author: Luhui Dev
summary: 🙋 I’m Luhui Dev , a developer who has been breaking down Agent engineering and exploring how AI can be applied in education. I focus on Agent Harness, LLM application engineering, AI for Math, and the productization of education SaaS. An Agent is a model-driven program that can use tools to complete a task. A customer service Agent , for example, can understand a refund request and call an order lookup API to check the purchase. Orchestration determines what happens first, which steps can run together, when a person needs to approve an action, and where each result goes. Agents, application code, and human approval can all participate. The diagram compares one typical use of each public framework from Microsoft, OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. Consider the same refund request in each case. Microsoft Agent Framework expresses explicit branches. The program verifies the order, requests approval, and waits for a person to decide whether it should proceed or send the case for manual handling. OpenAI Agents SDK offers two ways for Agents to work together. The support Agent can hand off the conversation to a refund specialist or ask that specialist to check eligibility and then reply itself. Google ADK lets code run steps in parallel. One branch checks the purchase date while another asks an Agent whether the complaint qualifies for a policy exception. The workflow combines both results. Claude Agent SDK lets the model choose its next action from tool results. It can look up the order, discover a previous contact, and read the old support ticket to gather enough information. Three questions help compare these approaches: Who decides what happens next, what does the runtime save, and what work repeats after a failure? Microsoft Agent Framework: Give approvals an explicit path Microsoft Agent Framework brings together AutoGen's multi-agent collaboration and Semantic Kernel's application integration foundations. [1] An Executor in a workflow can run code or an Agent. It handles incoming messages and sends its outputs downstream, which gives you a way to trace how a case moved through the workflow. After verifying an order, the verification executor sends a “case verified” message. The approval executor uses a RequestPort to issue an external request. If the reviewer answers the next day, the workflow can load a checkpoint and follow the appropriate branch for approval or rejection. With checkpointing enabled, the runtime saves workflow state and messages queued for the next round. You can test both paths with simulated approval messages. An approval should lead to execution, and a rejection should send the case for manual handling. An auditor can look up the decision without reconstructing the Agent's train of thought from a chat transcript. OpenAI Agents SDK: Two execution paths for one refund request Suppose a customer says, “I'd like a refund for the membership I bought yesterday.” The application passes the message and the support Agent to the SDK's Runner . The Runner calls the Agent's model, follows the tool calls or handoffs it requests, and continues the run. Developers configure which tools the support Agent can use and which Agents it can hand off to. Path one: Hand off to the refund Agent [2] Customer requests a refund → support Agent identifies the intent → Runner switches to the refund Agent → refund Agent looks up the order and replies The switch happens within the same run. The refund Agent becomes active and uses its own instructions and tools. If the order number is missing, it can ask the customer for it directly. Path two: Use the refund Agent as a tool to check eligibility Customer requests a refund → support Agent calls the refund Agent → refund Agent returns its eligibility finding → support Agent replies using that finding The tool call starts a subtask. Once the refund Agent reports that the order qualifies, the support Agent can check the refund status or reply directly. A handoff changes which Agent is active. Using an Agent as a tool delegates a piece of work and returns the result to the original Agent. If business rules require approval for large refunds, the application can enforce that rule and use RunState to preserve the paused run while the refund tool call awaits approval. Google ADK: If a condition will do, skip the model meeting Google ADK began with Agent hierarchies and built-in workflows for sequential, parallel, and loop execution. ADK 2.0 adds explicit workflow graphs . [3] Developers can put code and Agents in the same graph, specify which nodes run first and when edges can be followed, and pass structured outputs between nodes with events. The refund window and policy exceptions can be checked at the same time. One branch uses code to calculate the age of the order. The other asks an Agent to read the complaint and find the relevant policy clause. After receiving both results, the workflow applies the amount rule to decide whether the case needs approval. Downstream steps get the deadline check and the applicable policy clause without reading both full conversations again. Claude Agent SDK: Look at the evidence, then decide what to do Claude Agent SDK comes from Claude Code. It brings context management, tool calls, and permission controls into an ongoing tool loop. [4] When investigating a disputed refund, the Agent first reads the complaint and the order. If it finds that customer support promised compensation, it looks up the earlier ticket. If the case involves a policy that subsequently changed, it finds the version in force at the time. For larger investigations, the main Agent can ask several subagents to work in parallel. With the Workflow tool enabled, Claude can also write a task-specific JavaScript script for parallel checks, cross-checking, and synthesis, then pass it to the runtime. The plan can vary with the task, and the runtime schedules the steps expressed in the script. That flexibility suits investigation. When money is actually refunded, business rules should still control eligibility and payment approval. Final thoughts All four frameworks face the same trade-off. The clearer the rule, the more sense it makes to put it in code. The more a task depends on what turns up along the way, the more room the model needs to adapt its plan. Microsoft advances the workflow through messages. OpenAI lets Agents hand off a conversation or delegate a subtask. Google brings graph scheduling and Agents together. Claude can inspect a task and turn its plan into a script. title: Coordinates Before Geometry: Georeferencing, Reference Files and Unit Discipline
author: AIModelingDaily
summary: Every site model agrees with itself. That is the problem. Inside each tool, geometry is consistent. The terrain is smooth, the walls are vertical, the parts snap together. Then the terrain arrives in the drawing and sits 1.4 meters above the survey. Or an asset imports at one-twelfth scale. Or a reference file attaches at a rotation nobody remembers setting. None of these failures looks like a bug, because every individual tool did exactly what it was told. What failed was the coordinate contract. Geometry is the visible part of a site model and the least interesting part to debug. Coordinates are the part that decides whether the geometry is true. This article is about the contract and the checks that keep five different tools inside it: GenAnywhere for terrain, Archshaper for base maps, MicroStation for the record, Meshy for generated objects, and CityEngine for procedural context. The Contract Is Four Numbers Georeferencing sounds like an enterprise problem. It is four numbers and a statement of intent: A coordinate reference system, named and versioned. A linear unit, stated once and enforced everywhere. A vertical datum, stated separately from the horizontal one. A local origin, with a documented offset to the project control point. The intent is the sentence that says which of these is authoritative. In a site workflow, the survey control is authoritative. Everything else is aligned to it. Tools that generate geometry from maps or prompts are convenient, but none of them outranks the survey, and the moment that hierarchy flips, the model starts lying politely. Where Terrain Enters: GenAnywhere GenAnywhere is a terrain authoring environment. You sculpt surfaces in a browser, and the mesh stays coherent while you work. That coherence is about topology, not coordinates. A sculpted pad is a valid mesh in whatever local frame the tool is using. The contract obligation is therefore simple and easy to skip: record the transform between the authored terrain and the project CRS. If the tool exports in a local frame, export the offset with it. If it exports georeferenced, verify one known point against the survey before anyone designs on the surface. The check I run is a distance test between two control points measured in the terrain and measured on the survey. If the horizontal distance differs by more than 0.02 meters over 100 meters, something is off. At that point the cause is usually units or a projection mismatch, and finding it now costs minutes instead of a redesign. Where the Base Enters: Archshaper Archshaper generates 2D base maps from open map data and terrain, layered into buildings, roads, water, trees, and contours, and exports them with a controlled origin. That origin discipline is the reason the tool is usable at all. A base map with an arbitrary origin and a random rotation is not a base map; it is a background image that happens to have line weights. Two provenance facts belong in the manifest at this stage: the date of the source data and the state of the layers at export. A base exported in March and used in September is a claim about a neighborhood that has had six months to change. A base with trees merged into buildings cannot be separated later without redoing the export. The base also sets expectations. It is measured background, not a survey. Writing that sentence down prevents the most common downstream failure in civic work, which is a planning document inheriting map data at a precision it never had. Contours are a coordinate product, not decoration. If the surface and the contours disagree, the contours are the easier one to audit. Where the Record Enters: MicroStation MicroStation is where the model becomes a document. A DGN carries a geographic coordinate system, a reference structure, levels, and a design history. Those features are the reason the record can be audited while the study files cannot. The technical contract at this stage is the reference chain. Attach the survey, the base map, and the design geometry as separate references rather than merging them. Merging flattens provenance and makes every later correction a manual redo. Keep each reference on a named level structure, and keep one reference locked as the control. Two habits matter more than the settings. First, use the coordinate readout and precision input to place design geometry relative to control, not relative to the view. Second, snapshot the revision on the day the set is issued, and put the CRS, units, and revision in the file name and the issue note. A lock chamber is a coordinate problem with water in it. The wall tolerances do not care which tool modeled them. Where Assets Enter: Meshy Meshy generates objects from text prompts or reference images. It produces meshes with material maps and exports in standard interchange formats. What it does not produce is a coordinate system, a scale guarantee, or a survey relationship. That is acceptable for site furniture and unacceptable for anything measured. The contract rule is to normalize generated assets on import: apply a known scale, place them relative to a reference object, and record the intended dimensions in the manifest. An asset that imports at 0.08 scale and gets hand-resized in the scene is an asset with no dimensions at all. The second rule is classification. Generated objects are visual artifacts, not specification items. Tag them, keep them on their own layer, and exclude them from quantities and permit documents. A bench that looks correct and cannot be ordered is a rendering, not a product. Where Context Enters: CityEngine CityEngine generates surrounding urban fabric from written rules. Parcels, streets, and massing are produced procedurally, which means the context is only as trustworthy as the rules and the parcel data behind it. Coordinates enter here in a subtle way. Procedural context usually arrives at district scale, where small errors in origin or rotation are invisible locally and significant cumulatively. A block rotated half a degree away from the street grid will still look plausible in a rendering and will fail a shadow study, a wind study, or an emergency access review. The contract obligation is to anchor the procedural scene to the same CRS and origin as the record, and to version the rules alongside the model. A generated district whose rules are lost is a backdrop. A generated district whose rules are versioned is a tested assumption. A Manifest You Can Check The contract only works if it is executable. A small JSON manifest per stage is enough: { "project" : "riverfront_market" , "crs" : "EPSG:2255" , "horizontal_unit" : "us_survey_foot" , "vertical_datum" : "NAVD88" , "local_origin" : { "easting" : 2143550.42 , "northing" : 412880.17 , "elevation" : 6.31 } , "control_points" : [ { "id" : "CP-01" , "e" : 2143601.55 , "n" : 412914.02 , "z" : 6.44 } , { "id" : "CP-02" , "e" : 2143688.10 , "n" : 412842.77 , "z" : 5.98 } ] , "stages" : [ { "tool" : "archshaper" , "artifact" : "base_v03.dxf" , "date" : "2026-03-04" , "role" : "background" } , { "tool" : "genanywhere" , "artifact" : "terrain_opt_c.glb" , "date" : "2026-03-06" , "role" : "design_surface" } , { "tool" : "microstation" , "artifact" : "record_r07.dgn" , "date" : "2026-03-19" , "role" : "record" } , { "tool" : "meshy" , "artifact" : "furniture_set_02.glb" , "date" : "2026-03-20" , "role" : "visual_artifact" } , { "tool" : "cityengine" , "artifact" : "context_rules_v04" , "date" : "2026-03-22" , "role" : "context" } ] } And a check that runs on every export: import json , math def distance ( a , b ) : return math . sqrt ( ( a [ "e" ] - b [ "e" ] ) ** 2 + ( a [ "n" ] - b [ "n" ] ) ** 2 + ( a [ "z" ] - b [ "z" ] ) ** 2 ) manifest = json . load ( open ( "manifest.json" ) ) cp1 , cp2 = manifest [ "control_points" ] baseline = distance ( cp1 , cp2 ) for stage in manifest [ "stages" ] : if "measured_baseline" not in stage : continue delta = abs ( stage [ "measured_baseline" ] - baseline ) if delta > 0.02 : raise SystemExit ( f "{stage['artifact']}: baseline drift {delta:.3f} m. " "Check units and CRS before continuing." ) The numbers are illustrative, but the shape is the point. Every artifact declares its role, and every measured artifact proves it still agrees with control. Drift becomes a failing check instead of a discovery. The Three-Number Test If a team adopts nothing else from this article, adopt the test at the door: for every new artifact entering the model, state the CRS, the unit, and the vertical datum before the geometry loads. Three numbers, spoken aloud, written in the manifest. If the three numbers do not match the contract, the file does not enter. Most site model failures are not modeling failures. They are import failures that were never checked, discovered months later by someone measuring a dimension that felt wrong. Coordinates before geometry is not a slogan about precision. It is the order in which trust has to be established for any of the geometry to mean anything.

title: Z.ai Bets on Reused Layers to Make Frontier AI More Efficient
author: Jaromir Tesar
summary: Quick take Z.ai reports approximately 15% improvement on MMLU-Pro and 12% on GPQA-Diamond from a separate 30 billion parameter test model. Independent tester Nitish Garg found GLM-5.4 useful for code review and vulnerability hunting but substantially slower than Gemini 4 Neon. GLM-5.4 supports a 1 million token context window, different reasoning levels and availability across Z.ai’s Coding Plan tiers. The model is available through Z.ai Chat, ZCode and GLM Coding Plan, while API access is coming soon and open weights will follow safety hardening. Why it matters For developers and security teams, GLM-5.4 changes the choice from using one fast coding agent by default to reserving a slower, more capable reviewer for complex bugs and vulnerabilities. Its broader adoption will depend on API pricing, throughput, independent coding evaluations and whether Z.ai publishes open weights after safety hardening. Z.ai is betting that artificial intelligence can become more capable without becoming proportionally larger. Its GLM-5.4 model reuses the same 28 Transformer layers twice, increasing computation per token while avoiding a straightforward expansion of the network. The strategy could give Z.ai a cost and capability advantage, but early testing suggests the tradeoff may be slower responses and heavier inference workloads. A different route to scale Company-reported gains from a separate 30 billion parameter test model, not GLM-5.4 results — see the chart in the original article . Z.ai’s announcement of GLM-5.4 presents the model as the company’s first Loop Transformer and a move toward what it calls generalized coding. Rather than adding a new set of layers to increase depth, the architecture sends representations through the same 28 layers two times. That design gives GLM-5.4 a reported scale of 750 billion parameters while allowing Z.ai to claim a deeper effective computation path than a conventional model with the same layer count. The company says the approach is intended for tasks that require sustained, multi-step reasoning, including software engineering, cybersecurity, mechanical design, 3D modeling and physical control. The commercial logic is straightforward. Building ever-larger models requires more training infrastructure, memory and deployment capacity. Reusing layers could offer another way to improve performance without expanding every component of the model. If the technique works at scale, it could help Z.ai compete with much larger systems while reducing some of the pressure to increase parameter counts indefinitely. Z.ai also says GLM-5.4 adds vision capabilities to its coding-focused product line. The company describes inference-efficiency techniques alongside the Loop Transformer architecture , suggesting that the value of the design will depend not only on benchmark quality but also on whether the additional computation can be delivered at an acceptable cost. Evidence comes with important limits Z.ai reports results from a separate 30 billion parameter test model, not from the full 750 billion parameter GLM-5.4. In that test, the company says the looped architecture produced improvements of approximately 15% on MMLU-Pro and 12% on GPQA-Diamond. It identifies mathematics, scientific reasoning and long-context work as areas with particularly strong gains. Those results support the basic case for layer reuse, but they do not establish that the flagship model is superior across the coding tasks that will determine its commercial adoption. The public comparison material also does not fully explain its evaluation methodology, leaving outside users with limited information about how the reported improvements were measured. That distinction matters because GLM-5.4 is being positioned primarily as a tool for professional work. For developers and security teams, the relevant question is not simply whether the model can reason for longer. It is whether the added reasoning produces better code, fewer defects and stronger vulnerability analysis quickly enough to fit into existing workflows. Z.ai’s documentation confirms that GLM-5.4 is available across its Coding Plan tiers, supports a 1 million token context window and offers different reasoning levels. Early users see a capable but slow reviewer The most critical feedback has focused on that tradeoff. In independent testing reported by DataCamp , Nitish Garg found GLM-5.4 useful for code review and vulnerability hunting, but substantially slower than Gemini 4 Neon. The model reportedly used more reasoning steps and tokens, leading Garg to recommend it as a secondary reviewer rather than a default coding agent. That recommendation could limit Z.ai’s ability to turn technical capability into a broad business advantage. A model that catches subtle bugs or security flaws may be valuable as a specialist system, but many customers will still prioritize response speed, predictable costs and smooth integration with development tools. A reviewer that takes materially longer to complete a task may be used selectively instead of becoming the primary agent. The disagreement is therefore not about whether GLM-5.4 can be useful. Critics acknowledge its value in difficult review and security work. Their stronger argument is that usefulness alone does not prove the architecture is economically efficient. title: Signal #141: Agents Get Local Hands, Ruby and PHP Get Patched, and GitHub Closes a Trust Gap
author: The Dev Signal
summary: This week's cards cut across three layers of the stack: the local machine an agent can now reach, the runtimes and CI systems that are being hardened under our feet, and the data path that carries our prompts to inference providers. Two items demand action today, a Ruby heap overflow and a PHP session deserialization RCE, while the rest set up changes that are either already shipping or have fixed dates on the calendar. Raycast MCP lets agents control local Mac apps Enable Raycast MCP under Settings → MCP → Raycast MCP Server, add it to your agent app, and any MCP-capable client can reach Clipboard History, Snippets, Quicklinks, Focus, and browser tabs. Execution stays local, with no cloud relay in the middle, which is a meaningful difference from hosted tool servers that see your requests in transit. What matters is the permission surface. You opt in per extension, and the agent gets write access to clipboard, snippets, and app uninstall, which is more than a read-only convenience. That makes this a tool for replacing manual context-switching, not for exposing your whole desktop. Verdict: Evaluate. It's a shipped product and safe to try, but start with a narrow extension set and confirm what each one can mutate before you widen it. Ruby Case-Conversion Flaw Enables Heap Overflow Across Rails A one-byte heap overflow in legacy single-byte encodings is reachable through upcase , swapcase , downcase(:fold) , and casecmp? when the input is attacker-controlled. Default Rails and classic Sinatra apps hit the path through MethodOverride before authentication runs, so any app that parses a _method parameter is exposed. Bundled self-hosted products such as GitLab and Discourse inherit the risk until their Ruby runtime is rebuilt. The fixed releases are Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10. Ruby 3.2 and earlier are end of life and will not get this fix, so the upgrade path is the only real remediation for them. The Cloudflare WAF rules are a compensating control: they don't cover direct-to-origin traffic or non-HTTP entry points, so treat them as a bridge. Verdict: Ship now. Upgrade the runtime, then check distribution packages for backported fixes if you rely on system Ruby. PHP patches phpAfterShell RCE; Cloudflare WAF blocks attacks The fix for a CVSS 9.2 session-deserialization RCE is an upgrade to PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, or 8.6.0. Exposure is concentrated in deployments using the default file-based session handler on an affected version, and the advisory notes that real exploitability depends on conditions such as upload progress and serializer mismatches. Those conditions don't make the flaw safe to ignore; they just make it harder to scope. The hard part is inventory. PHP that arrives through CMS plugins or container images you don't rebuild directly is easy to miss. Linux distributions often backport fixes without bumping the version string, so compare the full package version against the distro advisory instead of trusting the number alone. The Cloudflare managed rules (Block by default on Free and paid plans, with the new PHP-FPM and SOAP rules set to Log) reduce exposure during rollout but cannot cover every path. Verdict: Ship now. Upgrade, restart every worker, and verify the package version against your distro's advisory rather than assuming the WAF has you covered. Dragos Canary Test Exposes Prompt Leakage Across Inference Providers The useful finding here is narrow: privacy flags like zdr: true govern the first hop only. Canary prompts seeded with fake credentials were mined for AWS keys within hours, and resellers on an open marketplace could read request data without any exploit. If your pipeline sends secrets to a model, the provider's retention setting is not the control you think it is. The mitigation is client-side. Put a scrubber in front of every LLM call, add per-request routing constraints such as data_collection: "deny" alongside zdr: true , and run pre-commit secret scanning so credentials don't enter prompts in the first place. Regex scrubbing is a seatbelt, not a guarantee, so layer it with seeded canaries that tell you when something leaks anyway. Verdict: Ship now as a layered control. Add redaction and per-request provider constraints to your agent and pipeline code, and audit existing accounts for ZDR coverage. GitHub blocks pull_request_target by default on December 2 Starting December 2, 2026, public repositories block pull_request_target by default, and organizations can enforce the block with a single policy. The risk is specific: a workflow that checks out fork pull request code under pull_request_target runs with read/write tokens and your secrets, so a stranger's PR can execute with your credentials. The Ultralytics and LiteLLM incidents are the cautionary cases. The migration is to move untrusted-ref workflows to the pull_request trigger, which runs fork code with a read-only token and no secrets. Before the cutoff, audit existing workflows, set the org-level event policy (Team/Enterprise) or the per-repo setting (Free), and check what the policy would block before you enforce it. The date is fixed, so the work has a deadline. Verdict: Ship now. Audit and migrate before December 2, and use the dry-run check to find breakage before enforcement does. Poppy 1.0 gives agents a standard business front door Poppy proposes a /.well-known/poppy.json file served over HTTPS so that agents acting for customers can identify themselves and learn what actions a business permits. Without a published file, a business is effectively invisible to Poppy-aware agents, and today's alternative is ad hoc scraping or undocumented API access. The protocol layers identity and permissions over existing MCP, OpenAPI, and UCP infrastructure rather than replacing them. The caveat is that this is draft 1.0, and the spec permits non-backward-compatible fixes. Serve the file, use OAuth for account-connected actions, validate against a test environment (the validator needs Node 22.18+), and pin your deployment to a specific revision. Re-validate after every spec change, because the file is cheap to publish and expensive to get wrong in production. Verdict: Evaluate. Worth publishing now for discoverability in a test environment, but treat the spec as unstable until it stops changing. If this kind of triage is useful to you, subscribe to Signal at https://repowrapped.com/signal , where we cover the tools and security changes that affect how senior engineers ship every week. We'll send the next issue when the cards are ready, not on a schedule we can't keep.
